title: Transformer Architecture Explained
objectives: Explain why Transformers replaced RNNs and LSTMs for language tasks.
Trace the data flow through a Transformer: embeddings, positional information, attention, feed-forward layers, residual connections and normalisation.
Compare encoder-only, decoder-only and encoder-decoder architectures with model examples.
Implement sinusoidal positional encoding and layer normalisation by hand.
Discuss the computational cost of Transformers and common modern refinements.
definition: The Transformer is a neural-network architecture, introduced in the 2017 paper 'Attention Is All You Need', that processes a whole sequence in parallel and uses self-attention to let every token gather information from every other token. It is built from stacked blocks of multi-head attention and feed-forward layers, joined by residual connections and layer normalisation, and it is the foundation of virtually all modern LLMs.

theory.heading: Why Transformers replaced RNNs
theory.body: Recurrent networks (RNNs, LSTMs) read text one token at a time, passing a hidden state forward. This is slow to train because steps cannot run in parallel, and information from early tokens fades over long distances. Transformers remove recurrence: all tokens are processed at once, and attention connects any two positions directly in a single step. This parallelism maps perfectly onto GPUs and made it practical to train models with billions of parameters on trillions of tokens.
points: Parallel training across the sequence instead of step-by-step recurrence.
Direct connections between distant tokens: no vanishing information path.
Scales smoothly with more data, parameters and compute.

theory.heading: Inside one Transformer block
theory.body: Input tokens are converted to embedding vectors and combined with positional information, because attention by itself has no sense of order. Each block then applies two sub-layers. Multi-head self-attention mixes information across tokens. A position-wise feed-forward network (two linear layers with a non-linearity such as GELU or SwiGLU, typically 4x wider than the model dimension) transforms each token independently. Each sub-layer is wrapped in a residual connection (x + sublayer(x)) and layer normalisation, which keep gradients stable in deep stacks. LLMs stack dozens of these blocks.
points: Token embedding + positional encoding -> N x [attention -> add & norm -> feed-forward -> add & norm].
Residual connections let gradients flow through very deep networks.
Modern LLMs use pre-norm (normalise before each sub-layer), often RMSNorm.

theory.heading: Positional information
theory.body: The original Transformer added fixed sinusoidal vectors to the embeddings: PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos / 10000^(2i/d)) and PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(pos / 10000^(2i/d)). Different dimensions oscillate at different frequencies, giving each position a unique pattern and making relative offsets easy to learn. BERT and GPT-2 used learned position embeddings. Most current LLMs (Llama, Qwen, Mistral) use Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE), which rotates query and key vectors according to position and extends better to long contexts.
points: Without positions, 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' look identical to attention.
Sinusoidal: fixed, no parameters. Learned: trained table. RoPE: rotation applied inside attention.
Context-extension techniques often work by rescaling RoPE frequencies.

theory.heading: Three architecture families
theory.body: Encoder-only models (BERT, RoBERTa) use bidirectional attention: every token sees the whole input, which is ideal for understanding tasks such as classification, NER and embeddings. Decoder-only models (GPT, Llama, Claude, Gemini) use causal (masked) attention: each token sees only earlier tokens, which suits next-token generation. Encoder-decoder models (original Transformer, T5, BART) encode the input bidirectionally and then generate output with a decoder that also attends to the encoder through cross-attention, useful for translation and summarisation.
points: Decoder-only: open-ended generation; the dominant LLM design today.
Encoder-decoder: sequence-to-sequence tasks with distinct input and output.

theory.heading: Cost and limitations
theory.body: Self-attention compares every token with every other token, so its compute and memory grow quadratically with sequence length (O(n^2)). This is the main reason long contexts are expensive. Engineering advances such as FlashAttention (memory-efficient exact attention), grouped-query attention (fewer key/value heads), the KV cache, and Mixture-of-Experts layers (activating only some feed-forward experts per token) make large Transformers practical to train and serve.
points: Quadratic attention cost in sequence length.
Parameters mostly live in the feed-forward layers and embeddings.
Alternatives such as state-space models (Mamba) aim for linear-time sequence processing.

example.title: Inspecting a real Transformer's configuration
example.body: Hugging Face exposes each model's architecture settings. Loading only the configuration (no weights) shows the number of layers, hidden size, attention heads and maximum positions. For GPT-2 small: 12 layers, a hidden size of 768, 12 heads and 1,024 positions.

code.source:
from transformers import AutoConfig

cfg = AutoConfig.from_pretrained('gpt2')
print(cfg.n_layer, cfg.n_embd, cfg.n_head, cfg.n_positions)
# 12 768 12 1024

cfg = AutoConfig.from_pretrained('bert-base-uncased')
print(cfg.num_hidden_layers, cfg.hidden_size, cfg.num_attention_heads)
# 12 768 12  (encoder-only)

use_cases.title: Text generation
use_cases.description: Decoder-only Transformers power chat assistants, coding assistants and content tools.

use_cases.title: Understanding and search
use_cases.description: Encoder-only models produce embeddings and classify text for search, moderation and routing.

use_cases.title: Translation and summarisation
use_cases.description: Encoder-decoder models such as T5 and mBART map an input sequence to a different output sequence.

use_cases.title: Beyond text
use_cases.description: Vision Transformers treat image patches as tokens; audio and protein models use the same block design.

demonstration.description: Follow the shape of the data through a tiny decoder-only Transformer with a model dimension of 512 for a 6-token input. Shapes stay the same through every block until the final projection to vocabulary logits.

code.source:
Input text: "Transformers changed natural language processing" -> 6 token IDs
Embedding lookup         : (6,) -> (6, 512)
+ positional information : (6, 512)
Block 1..N (attention + FFN, residual, norm): (6, 512) -> (6, 512)
Final norm + output projection: (6, 512) -> (6, 50000)

demonstration.output: One row of 50,000 logits per position. During generation only the last row is used: softmax over it gives the next-token distribution.

takeaways: Transformers process sequences in parallel and connect all tokens with self-attention.
A block = multi-head attention + feed-forward network, each with a residual connection and normalisation.
Positional information (sinusoidal, learned or RoPE) supplies word order.
Encoder-only for understanding, decoder-only for generation, encoder-decoder for seq2seq.
Attention cost grows quadratically with sequence length; FlashAttention, GQA and the KV cache help.
Most LLM parameters sit in feed-forward layers and embeddings.

interview.question: What problem did the Transformer solve compared with RNNs?
interview.answer: RNNs process tokens sequentially, which prevents parallel training and weakens long-range dependencies. Transformers use self-attention over all tokens at once, enabling parallel training on GPUs and direct connections between distant tokens.
interview.explanation: Mention both parallelism and long-range dependencies; these are the two points interviewers look for.

interview.question: Describe the components of a Transformer block.
interview.answer: Multi-head self-attention followed by a position-wise feed-forward network, each wrapped with a residual connection and layer normalisation. Input embeddings carry positional information.
interview.explanation: A strong answer also notes pre-norm vs post-norm and that modern LLMs use RMSNorm and SwiGLU.

interview.question: Why does a Transformer need positional encoding?
interview.answer: Self-attention treats its input as a set: it is permutation-invariant. Positional encodings inject order so the model can distinguish 'dog bites man' from 'man bites dog'.
interview.explanation: Name the three main approaches: sinusoidal, learned absolute and rotary (RoPE).

interview.question: Compare BERT, GPT and T5 architecturally.
interview.answer: BERT is encoder-only with bidirectional attention, trained with masked language modelling. GPT is decoder-only with causal attention, trained on next-token prediction. T5 is encoder-decoder, framing every task as text-to-text.
interview.explanation: Link each architecture to the tasks it suits best; this is one of the most common GenAI interview questions.

interview.question: What is the computational complexity of self-attention and why does it matter?
interview.answer: O(n^2 * d) for sequence length n and dimension d, because every token attends to every other. Doubling context length roughly quadruples attention compute and memory, which drives the cost of long-context models.
interview.explanation: Mention mitigations (FlashAttention, sliding-window or sparse attention, KV cache) to show awareness of production concerns.

interview.question: What is the role of residual connections and layer normalisation?
interview.answer: Residual connections add each sub-layer's input to its output, giving gradients a direct path and letting deep stacks train. Layer normalisation rescales activations per token to zero mean and unit variance, stabilising training.
interview.explanation: Advanced candidates mention that pre-norm placement trains more stably at depth, which is why modern LLMs use it.

practice.title: Positional encoding and layer normalisation
practice.objective: Implement two building blocks of a Transformer: adding sinusoidal positional encodings to embeddings and applying layer normalisation.
practice.statement: You receive n token embeddings of dimension d (d is even). For each position pos (starting at 0) compute the sinusoidal positional encoding: PE[2i] = sin(pos / 10000^(2i/d)) and PE[2i+1] = cos(pos / 10000^(2i/d)) for i = 0 .. d/2 - 1. Add it to the embedding to get x. Then apply layer normalisation without learnable parameters: ln = (x - mean(x)) / sqrt(var(x) + 1e-5), where var is the population variance over the d values. Print x and ln for every position.
practice.input_format:
Line 1: n d.
Next n lines: d numbers, the embedding of each token.
practice.output_format:
For each position p, two lines: x

: ln

: Never print -0.0000.
constraints: Round each printed value to 4 decimals.
practice.solution:
import math

n, d = map(int, input().split())
rows = [list(map(float, input().split())) for _ in range(n)]

def fmt(values):
    return ' '.join(f'{round(v, 4) + 0.0:.4f}' for v in values)

def positional_encoding(pos, d):
    pe = [0.0] * d
    for i in range(d // 2):
        angle = pos / (10000 ** (2 * i / d))
        pe[2 * i] = math.sin(angle)
        pe[2 * i + 1] = math.cos(angle)
    return pe

for pos, emb in enumerate(rows):
    x = [e + p for e, p in zip(emb, positional_encoding(pos, d))]
    mean = sum(x) / d
    var = sum((v - mean) ** 2 for v in x) / d
    ln = [(v - mean) / math.sqrt(var + 1e-5) for v in x]
    print(f'x{pos}: {fmt(x)}')
    print(f'ln{pos}: {fmt(ln)}')
explanation: For each pair of dimensions (2i, 2i+1) compute one angle pos / 10000^(2i/d); even indices take its sine and odd indices its cosine.
Low dimensions oscillate quickly and high dimensions slowly, so each position gets a unique fingerprint.
Add the encoding element-wise to the token embedding, exactly as the original Transformer does before the first block.
Layer normalisation subtracts the mean of the d values and divides by the standard deviation (with a small epsilon for stability).
Format with rounding and + 0.0 so a tiny negative number does not print as -0.0000.

quiz.question: Which property of Transformers made large-scale training on GPUs practical?
options: They process all tokens of a sequence in parallel
They only work on short sentences
quiz.explanation: Removing recurrence lets all positions be computed at once, which maps well onto GPU parallelism.

quiz.question: Which model is encoder-only?
quiz.explanation: BERT uses only the encoder stack with bidirectional attention; GPT and Llama are decoder-only, and T5 is encoder-decoder.

quiz.question: Using sinusoidal positional encoding, what is the value of dimension 0 (the first sine) at position 0?
quiz.explanation: PE(0, 0) = sin(0 / 10000^0) = sin(0) = 0. The paired cosine dimension would be 1.

quiz.question: You double a model's input length from 4K to 8K tokens. Roughly how does the self-attention compute change?
options: It doubles exactly, like the feed-forward layers
quiz.explanation: Attention is quadratic in sequence length: (2n)^2 = 4n^2.

quiz.question: In a Transformer block, what does the expression x + attention(norm(x)) implement?
quiz.code:
def block(x):
    x = x + attention(norm(x))
    x = x + ffn(norm(x))
    return x
options: A pre-norm residual connection around the attention sub-layer
quiz.explanation: The input is normalised, passed through attention and added back to the original x: a residual connection in pre-norm style.
